label: prop1
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As $u\in L^2(B_R^c(0)),$ the condition in~\eqref{eqn37.101} is
  satisfied for both $+$ and $-,$ which then implies {\color{black} by the
    propagation of singularities as noted above} \color{black} that
  $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)=\emptyset.$ Therefore $u$ is Schwartz in a
  neighborhood of infinity. The proof in~\cite{VasyAsterisque} that
  such a solution vanishes faster than any exponential is local at
  infinity. Moreover, the Carleman estimate {\color{black}
    in~\cite{VasyAsterisque}} \color{black} showing that a
  super-exponentially vanishing solution is actually zero in a
  neighborhood of infinity is also local at infinity. Hence $u$
  vanishes in an open set. The classical unique continuation theorems
  for second order elliptic operators then imply that $u$ vanishes in
  $B_R^c(0).$
head: environment

label: thm2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm2}
    If the metric $g,$  and the operator $H_{\rho,q}$ satisfy
    the hypotheses above, then, for $k_0\in (0,\infty),$ a solution $u$ to
    $(H_{\rho,q}+k_0^2)u=0,$ for which $\operatorname{WF}^{*,l}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)\cap R^-_{k^2_0}=\emptyset,$ (or
    $\operatorname{WF}^{*,l}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)\cap R^+_{k^2_0}=\emptyset$), for an $l>
    -\frac 12,$ has
    $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)\subset
    R^+_{k^2_0}$ (resp. $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)\subset
    R^-_{k^2_0}$) and therefore  $u\equiv 0.$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The outgoing condition on $\operatorname{mf}$ can be checked by evaluating the
    asymptotic decay rate of $(\partial_r-ik_0)u(r\omega);$ it is checked
    near the front faces by applying operators like those
    in~\eqref{eqn41.333}. In~\cite{VasyAsterisque,VasyExpDecay} the
    Mourre estimate, at any negative eigenvalue, is proved for
    operators like $H_{\rho,q}$. The absence of point spectrum
    embedded in the continuum is also established. Using standard
    arguments, this gives a proof of the limiting absorption principle,
    along with the fact that the limiting absorption solution to
    \begin{equation}
      (H_{\rho,q}+k_0^2)u=f\in (1+r^2)^{-\frac{l}{2}}L^2(\mathbb R^d),\, l>\frac 12,
    \end{equation}
    is outgoing.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
{\color{black} See the paragraph of
      \eqref{eqn37.101-pre}-\eqref{eqn37.101} for the proof that $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}^{m,l}(u)\subset
    R^+_{k^2_0}$ (resp. $\operatorname{WF} ^{m,l}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)\subset
    R^-_{k^2_0}$) for $l<-1/2$. By a result of Isozaki
  \cite[Lemma~4.5]{Isozaki94}, as presented in
  \cite[Proposition~17.8]{VasyAsterisque}, which strongly uses
    that $u$ satisfies the homogeneous equation,  for such a
  $u,$ $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}^{m,l}(u)=\emptyset$ for  $l\in(-1/2,0).$ Hence
  the radial point estimate of \cite{VasyAsterisque} strengthens
  this to all $l$. At this point Proposition~\ref{prop1} is applicable and shows
  that $u$ vanishes near infinity. The classical unique continuation theorems
  for second order elliptic operators then imply that $u$ vanishes.}
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
If $u\in L^2(B_r^c(0))$ is a solution to
    $H_{\rho,q}u+k_0^2u=0,$ for an $\omega>0,$ then $u\equiv 0.$
    Hence such an $L^2$-solution to $\widetilde{H}_{c,\rho}u+\omega^2u=0$ is also
    identically zero.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In~\eqref{eqn27.2} we give a generalized eigenvalue problem implied
  by Maxwell's equation, with an operator that is independent of
  $\omega,$ whereas in~\eqref{eqn27.1}, we formulate it as a standard
  eigenvalue problem, but in terms of an operator that also depends on
  $\omega.$ We generally use the latter formulation as it fits more
  closely with earlier work.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The first order term
  $$\widehat{N}_{\operatorname{ff}_j,0}(Q_1^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j})(\tau)=\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{11}+
  \tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10},$$
  where $\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{11}$ is a
  first order operator and $\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10}$ is zeroth order.
  Because of the term $\tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10},$ these operators do
  not have the product structure required in earlier versions of
  Vasy's theorem. In particular the proof of the Mourre estimate needs
  to be modified.  In Section~\ref{ss.mourre} we introduce a Mourre
  estimate for $N$-body Schr\"odinger operators that allows terms like
  $\tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10}$ in the indicial operators at the front
  faces. A simplified proof for the wave-guide case is given in
  Appendix~\ref{MourreEstMaxWG}. A proof of the general result,
  following the argument in~\cite{VasyAsterisque,VasyExpDecay}, is
  given in Appendix~\ref{MourreEstGenCase}.  The Mourre estimate is
  the essential step needed to establish radiation conditions for
  Maxwell wave-guides.

title: Remark
body_md:
In the wave-guide literature the parameter values
  $\{\tau_{jk}^{1}\}$ for which non-trivial $L^2$-solutions
  to~\eqref{eqn48.61} exist are called \emph{propagation constants},
  as $\omega/\tau^{1}_{jk}$ is the phase velocity down the
  wave-guide of the corresponding mode. For consistency with the
  preceding discussion we continue to call them wave-guide
  frequencies. We let
  \begin{equation}
    \mathcal T_1=\bigcup_{j=1}^m\{\pm \tau^{1}_{jk}:\:k=1,\dots,N_j^{1}\}
  \end{equation}
  denote the totality of wave-guide frequencies for 1-forms.

label: prop2.224
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop2.224}
     Assume that $0\notin\sigma_{\operatorname{pp}}(L_{\pm\sqrt{\lambda},j}).$ For
     each $j$ there is an integer $N^{1}_j(\lambda),$ so that there
     are $N^{1}_j(\lambda)$ positive values
     $\{\tau^1_{jk}(\lambda):\:k=1\cdots,N^1_j(\lambda)\}$ and
                         
      eigenpairs
     $\{(\pm\tau^{1}_{jk}(\lambda),\check{\xi}^{\pm}_{jk}(\lambda)):\:k=1,\dots,
     N^{1\,\pm}_j(\lambda)\},$ such that
  \begin{equation}\label{eqn49.60}
     \left[
     L_{\tau^{1}_{jk}(\lambda),j}+(\tau^{1}_{jk}(\lambda))^2\right]
   \check{\xi}^{\pm}_{jk}(\lambda)=\lambda \check{\xi}^{\pm}_{jk}(\lambda),
  \end{equation}
  and these forms span the $L^2$-solutions
  to~\eqref{eqn49.60}.  The values of
  $\tau$ for which such a solution exists have $|\tau|$ in an interval
  $(\sqrt{\lambda},\tau_{\max}].$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The notations $N^1_j, \tau^1_{jk},\check{\xi}^{\pm}_{jk},$ etc. refer to
     the special case $\lambda=\omega^2\kappa_0^2,$  which is covered
     in Proposition~\ref{propNew2}.
head: environment

label: eqn108.225
title: Remark
body_md:
In the proof we show that
  \begin{equation}\label{eqn108.225}
    N_{\max}(\lambda)=\max\{N^{1}_j(\lambda):\: j=1,\dots,m\},
  \end{equation}
  the maximum number of $L^2$-solutions to~\eqref{eqn49.60} for any channel, is
  finite. This follows from the fact that the number of non-positive
  eigenvalues of the operators $L_{\tau,j},$ for
  $|\tau|\in[\sqrt{\lambda},\tau_{\max}]$ is uniformly bounded and the
  analytic dependence of the negative eigenvalues on $\tau.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $L_{-\tau,j}=\overline{L_{\tau,j}},$ we know that
  $\sigma_{\operatorname{pp}}(L_{\tau,j})=\sigma_{\operatorname{pp}}(L_{-\tau,j}),$ and so it
  suffices to consider $\tau>0.$ That all $\tau^{1}_{jk}(\lambda)\geq
  \sqrt{\lambda}$ follows from the fact that the perturbation terms,
  $\widetilde{Q}_1^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}(\tau)+
  \widetilde{Q}_0^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}+\omega^2(\kappa_0^2-\kappa_j^2),$ are
  compactly supported. Therefore an $L^2$-solution to~\eqref{eqn49.60}
  in the complement of ball can only exist if $(\lambda-\tau^2)\leq
  0.$
                   
                                                               
                                               

  We rewrite
  $$\widetilde{Q}_1^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}(\tau)=\tau\widetilde{Q}_{10}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}+\widetilde{Q}_{11}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j},\text{ and }
   \widehat{Q}_0^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}= \widetilde{Q}_0^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}+\omega^2(\kappa_0^2-\kappa_j^2).$$
  For a variable $\tau,$ we express the condition in~\eqref{eqn49.60}
  in the weak form
  \begin{multline}
  \int_{\mathbb R^2}  \left[\left|d\check{\xi}\right|^2+  \left|d^* \check{\xi}\right|^2+ \left\langle
          [\widetilde{Q}_{11}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}+\widehat{Q}_{0}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}]
          \check{\xi}, \check{\xi}\right\rangle\right]dx= \\
  \int_{\mathbb R^2}\langle
 [\lambda-\tau^2-\tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10}]\check{\xi}, \check{\xi}\rangle dx.
  \end{multline}
  
 The left hand side is a compactly supported perturbation of the Dirichlet
 form, and so is bounded below by $-M\| \check{\xi}\|^2,$ for a finite $M.$
 On the other hand, the quadratic dependence of
 $\lambda-\tau^2-\tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10}$ allows
 the r.h.s. to become an arbitrarily large, negative multiple of
 $\|\check{\xi}\|^2,$ as $|\tau|\to\infty.$ Hence there is a $\tau_{\max}$
 as stated in the proposition. We say that the value of $\tau$ is
 \emph{allowed} if $|\tau|\in[\sqrt{\lambda},\tau_{\max}].$
   
For each $\tau$ in the allowed intervals, the operator $L_{\tau,j}$ has
finitely many negative eigenvalues $\{\lambda_l(\tau)\}.$ A simple
comparison argument using the min-max principle shows that there is an
integer $J$ so that, for $|\tau|\leq \tau_{\max},$ there are at most $J$
such eigenvalues.  The proposition follows once we show that the curve
$\{(\tau,\lambda-\tau^2):|\tau|\leq \tau_{\max}\}$
intersects these finitely many curves, $\{(\tau,\lambda_l(\tau))\}$ in
a finite number of points $\{\tau^{1}_{jl}(\lambda):\:l=1,\dots,
N^{1}_j\}.$

 First assume that $L_{\tau,j}$ does not have resonances at
 $\sqrt{\lambda}.$ In this case we only need to consider intersections between
 strictly negative eigenvalue branches defined for
 $|\tau|\in(\lambda,\tau_{\max}]$ and the curve
   $$\mathcal{C}_p=\{(\tau,\lambda-\tau^2): \omega\kappa_0<|\tau|<
   \tau_{\max}\}.$$ In particular such an eigenvalue is less than $0$
   and therefore we can use analytic perturbation theory,
   see~\cite{Kato}, to conclude that there are analytic functions
   $(\lambda(\tau),u(\tau)),$ such that
 \begin{equation}
   L_{\tau}u(\tau)=\lambda(\tau)u(\tau)\text{ with }\|u(\tau)\|^2_{L^2}=1.
 \end{equation}
 A standard calculation shows that
 \begin{equation}\label{eqn110.223}
   \dot{\lambda}(\tau)=\langle \dot{L}_{\tau}u(\tau),u(\tau)\rangle=
   \langle \widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10}u(\tau),u(\tau)\rangle
   =-4\operatorname{Im}\langle \check{\xi}_{1\tau},d\mathfrak l\lrcorner\breve{\xi}_{\tau}\rangle,
 \end{equation}
 and therefore,  we have the
 estimate
 \begin{equation}\label{eqn138.400}
   \begin{split}
     |\dot{\lambda}(\tau)|<&4\|d\mathfrak l\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\check{\xi}_{1\tau}\|(\|\check{\xi}_{2\tau}\|
     +\|\check{\xi}_{3\tau}\|)\\
     &<2\sqrt{2}\|d\mathfrak l\|_{L^{\infty}}.
     \end{split}
 \end{equation}
 
 This shows that it is impossible for a branch to satisfy
 $\lambda_l(\tau)=\lambda-\tau^2.$ A simple compactness
 argument, combined with the bound on the maximum number of
 eigenvalues, for any allowable $\tau,$ and the fact that eigenvalue
 branches can only appear, or disappear at $\lambda=0,$ and therefore
 have analytic representations,
 finishes the proof in the non-resonance case.

 Now suppose that $L_{\tau,j}$ has a resonance at $\sqrt{\lambda};$
 for definiteness assume that there are analytic functions
 $(\lambda_0(\tau),v_0(\tau))$ defined in
 $(\sqrt{\lambda},\sqrt{\lambda}+\epsilon)$ for an $\epsilon>0,$ with
 \begin{equation}\label{eqn112.223}
 L_{\tau,j}v_0(\tau)=\lambda_0(\tau)v_0(\tau),   
 \end{equation}
 and
 \begin{equation}
   \lim_{\tau\to[\omega\kappa_0]^+}\lambda_0(\tau)=0\text{ and }\|v_0(\tau)\|_{L^2}=1.
 \end{equation}
 
 The sequence $\{v_0(\tau)\}$ must converge weakly to zero as
 $\tau\to[\sqrt{\lambda}]^+,$ otherwise the (non-zero) limit would be
 an $L^2$-eigenfunction of $L_{\tau,j}$ with eigenvalue equal to zero,
 which we have excluded. The Rellich theorem, elliptic regularity,
 and~\eqref{eqn112.223} imply that, for any $R>0,$
 $v_0(\tau)\upharpoonright_{B_R(0)}$ converges strongly to zero. Since
 $\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon_j,\mu_j}_{10}$ is compactly
 supported,~\eqref{eqn110.223} implies that
 \begin{equation}
   \lim_{\tau\to[\omega\kappa_0]^+}\dot{\lambda}_0(\tau)=0.
 \end{equation}
 Using the mean value theorem, we easily conclude that there cannot be
 an infinite sequence $\tau_l\to[\sqrt{\lambda}]^+,$ where
 \begin{equation}\label{eqn116.234}
   \tau_l^2+\lambda_0(\tau_l)-\lambda=0,
 \end{equation}
 see Remark~\ref{rmk5.333}. Hence there is a smallest
 $\tau_1>\sqrt{\lambda}$ where
 \begin{equation}
    \lambda_0(\tau_1)=\lambda-\tau_1^2<0.
 \end{equation}

label: eqn118.223
title: Remark
body_md:
The proposition shows that there for each $j$ and
  $0<\lambda,$ there is a non-negative number
  $\gamma_j(\lambda)$ so that
  \begin{equation}
    \gamma_j(\lambda)=\min\{[\pm\tau_{jk}^{1}(\lambda)]^2-\lambda:\: k=1,\dots,N_j^{1}\}.
  \end{equation}
  If this number is positive, then we say that $\gamma_j(\lambda)$ is the
  \emph{gap at the bottom of the continuous spectrum} of the family
  $L_{\tau,j}$ at the eigenvalue $\lambda.$ Suppose that $L_{\tau,j}$
  has a resonance at $\pm\sqrt{\lambda};$ let $\tau_{\delta}$ denote
  the solutions
  \begin{equation}\label{eqn118.223}
    -\lambda_0(\tau_{\delta})=\lambda+\delta-\tau^2_{\delta},
  \end{equation}
  for small $\delta.$ It is clear that $\lim_{\delta\to
    0}\lambda_0(\tau_{\delta})=0.$ So that the family of operators
  $L_{\tau,j}$ does not have a uniform sized gap at the bottom of the
  continuous spectrum at  $\tau=\sqrt{\lambda+\delta},$ as
  $\delta\to 0.$ A similar situation can also arise at
  $\tau=-\sqrt{\lambda}.$

  For our simplified proof of the Mourre inequality for wave-guides we
  assume that, for some $\delta_0>0,$ the ``family'' gap:
  \begin{equation}\label{eqn119.224}
    \Gamma(\lambda,\delta_0)=\inf\{\gamma_j(\lambda+\alpha):\:
    |\alpha|\leq\delta_0, j=1,\dots,m\}
  \end{equation}
  is positive. This will be the case, for some $\delta_0>0,$ if and
  only if the families $\{L_{\tau,j}:\: j=1,\dots,m\}$ do not have
  have  families of eigenvalues $\lambda_0(\tau)$ converging to $0$ as
  $\tau\to\pm\sqrt{\lambda}.$
head: environment

label: rmk5.333
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk5.333}
  If  $0\in\sigma_{\operatorname{pp}}(L_{\pm\sqrt{\lambda},j}),$ then
  there may or may not be a branch of negative eigenvalues
  $\lambda(\tau),$ for $\pm\tau\in
  (\sqrt{\lambda},\sqrt{\lambda}+\delta),$ converging to $0$ as
  $\tau\to\sqrt{\lambda}.$  If no such such branch exists then the
  results of Proposition~\ref{prop2.224} clearly remain true. If such
  a branch exists, then it still follows from~\eqref{eqn110.223} that
  the limits
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{\tau\to\pm\omega\kappa_0^{\pm}}\dot{\lambda}(\tau)=d
  \end{equation}
  exist. If there were infinitely many roots $\{\tau_l\}$ (for
  definiteness greater than $\sqrt{\lambda}$) to the equation
  in~\eqref{eqn116.234}, then the mean value theorem implies that
  there is an infinite  sequence $\tau_{l+1}<\tau'_{l}<\tau_{l}$ so
  that
  \begin{equation}
    \dot{\lambda}(\tau'_l)=-2\tau_l'.
  \end{equation}
  This would imply that
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{\tau\to \omega\kappa_0^+}\dot{\lambda}(\tau)=-2\sqrt{\lambda}.
  \end{equation}
  If $\sqrt{2}\|d\mathfrak l\|_{L^{\infty}}<\sqrt{\lambda},$
  then~\eqref{eqn138.400} shows that this is not possible, and again
  the conclusion of the theorem holds in this case. Hence the
  conclusion holds for sufficiently large energies.

  Of particular interest is the case $\lambda=\omega^2\kappa_0^2.$
  Even if $\sqrt{2}\|d\mathfrak l\|_{L^{\infty}}>\omega\kappa_0,$
  Proposition~\ref{propNew2} implies that there cannot be infinitely many
  solutions to $\lambda(\tau)=\omega^2\kappa_0^2-\tau^2.$

label: RadCondMax
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{RadCondMax}    If
    $\mathcal H^{\epsilon,\mu}_{\omega}$ satisfies a Mourre estimate at
    $k_0^2=\omega^2\kappa^2_0,$ and $\omega\notin\mathcal E,$ 
    then    a solution $\tilde{\xi},$ $\tilde{\eta}$ resp. to
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn131.337}
      \kappa^2\mathcal{D}^{\epsilon,\mu}_1\tilde{\xi}=\omega^2\kappa^2\tilde{\xi},\quad
      \kappa^2\mathcal{D}^{\epsilon,\mu}_2\tilde{\eta}=\omega^2\kappa^2\tilde{\eta}\text{ resp. }
    \end{equation}
    for which the components satisfy the classical Sommerfeld
    radiation condition along $\operatorname{mf}$ and such that
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn132.337}
      \operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}^{*,l}(\tilde{\xi})\cap R^{1,-}_{k_0^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}=\emptyset,\quad
       \operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}^{*,l}(\tilde{\eta})\cap R^{2,-}_{k_0^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}=\emptyset\text{ resp.},
    \end{equation}
    for $j=1,\dots, m,$ and an $l>-\frac 12,$ is identically zero.

    If $\omega\in\mathcal E,$ then such solutions belong to finite
    dimensional spaces of $L^2$-eigenfunctions. The set $\mathcal E$ is
    discrete.

title: Corollary
body_md:
Assume that $\mathcal H^{\epsilon,\mu}_{\omega}$ satisfies a Mourre estimate at
    $\omega^2\kappa^2_0,$ and $\omega\notin\mathcal E;$ let $(\xi,\eta)$ be a
    solution to Maxwell's equations~\eqref{eqn7}. If the pair
    $(\xi,\eta)$ satisfies the Sommerfeld radiation condition over
    $\operatorname{mf},$ with $k_0=\omega\kappa_0,$ and the conditions
    in~\eqref{eqn132.337}, then $(\xi,\eta)=(0,0).$ If $\omega\in\mathcal E,$
    then such a solution belongs to a finite dimensional space of
    Schwartz class eigenfunctions.

label: def:microlocal-Mourre-loss
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:microlocal-Mourre-loss}
We say that the effective microlocal Mourre loss at energy $\lambda$
at $(y_a,\xi_a)$, $\delta^a(y_a,\xi_a;\lambda)$, is given as follows: let
$\lambda'=\lambda-|\xi_a|^2$  with spectral
projector $E$ of $H^a(y_a,\xi_a)$ to $\lambda'$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item
  If $E$ is finite rank (including if $\lambda'$ is not an eigenvalue) we set $\delta^a(y_a,\xi_a;\lambda)=0$,
  \item
$E$ is infinite rank and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mourre-strongly-adapted-compact}
E\Big[\frac{\xi_a}{|\xi_a|}\partial_{\xi_a},H^a\Big]E
\end{equation}
is compact on $L^2(X^a)$, we set $\delta^a(y_a,\xi_a;\lambda)=0$.
\item
  Otherwise $\delta^a(y_a,\xi_a;\lambda)$ is the inf of constants so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mourre-strongly-adapted}
\Big\||\xi_a|E\Big[\frac{\xi_a}{|\xi_a|}\partial_{\xi_a},H^a\Big]E\Big\|\leq  \delta^a(y_a,\xi_a;\lambda).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

We say that the effective Mourre loss at the level of a subsystem
$a\in\mathcal{A}$ at energy $\lambda$ is
$$
\delta^a(\lambda)=\sup_{(y_a,\xi_a)}\delta^a(y_a,\xi_a;\lambda),
$$
understood to be $0$ if $\lambda-|\xi_a|^2\notin \sigma_{\operatorname{pp}}(H^a(y_a,\xi_a))$ for all
$(y_a,\xi_a)$.

label: eqn128.222
title: Theorem
body_md:
Fix a $c_0>0,$ and 
 assume that~\eqref{eqn136.224} holds.  Given
 $\lambda\in\mathcal I_M(c_0),$ 
there are positive constants $C_0$ and $\delta<\delta_0,$ so
that if $\phi\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}_c(\mathbb R)$ has $\operatorname{supp}\phi\subset
(\lambda-\delta,\lambda+\delta),$ with $\phi(t)=1$,\hspace{2 pt} for $
t\in (\lambda-\frac{\delta}{2},\lambda+\frac{\delta}{2}),$ then
\begin{equation}\label{eqn128.222}
  i\langle\phi(H)[A,H]\phi(H)\psi,\psi\rangle\geq
  C_0\|\phi(H)\psi\|^2+
  \langle\psi, K\psi\rangle,
\end{equation}
where $K$ is a compact operator.

title: Remark
body_md:
The argument given below also works at $\lambda=\omega^2\kappa_0^2$
  if the contrast ratios satisfy the estimate
  in~\eqref{cntrst_ratio_est}. For simplicity we give the proof under
  assumption $\lambda\in\mathcal I_M,$ but see Remark~\ref{rmk14.700}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the proof we follow the approach taken in~\cite[Chapter
    12]{VasyAsterisque}, which reduces the proof of the global
  estimate~\eqref{eqn128.222} to proving uniform estimates, at
  infinity in $\overline{\mathbb R}^3_{\operatorname{WG}}$ for the indicial operators,
  $i\widehat{N}_{a,0}([A,H])(\tau),$ where $a=\operatorname{mf}$ or $\operatorname{ff}_j,\,j=1,\dots,m.$
  The argument with $a=\operatorname{mf}$ is trivial because $H$ equals the
  Euclidean Laplacian in a neighborhood of $\operatorname{mf},$ and therefore
  $i[A,H]=2H.$ We focus on the estimates along the front faces.

  Recall that in a neighborhood of $\operatorname{ff}_j$ the coefficients
  $\epsilon_j,\mu_j$ depend only variables orthogonal to the channel
  direction. We fix a value of $j$ and introduce coordinates so that
  the channel is $\{x_1>r,\, x_2=x_3=0\}.$ To simplify the notation we
  also drop the $j$-subscripts. As coordinates near the
  front face we use
  \begin{equation}
    \rho=\frac{1}{x_1},\,(Y_1,Y_2)=(x_2,x_3).
  \end{equation}
We observe that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn158.502}
  \begin{split}
    i\widehat{N}_{\operatorname{ff},0}([A,H])(\tau)&=[\widehat{N}_{\operatorname{ff},0}(H)(\tau),Y\cdot\partial_{Y}]+2\tau^2+
    \tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon,\mu}_{10}\\
    &=[\widehat{N}_{\operatorname{ff},0}(H)(\tau),Y\cdot\partial_{Y}]+\tau\partial_{\tau}\widehat{N}_{\operatorname{ff},0}(H)(\tau).
    \end{split}
  \end{equation}
  Because of the term $\tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon,\mu}_{10},$ this differs from
  the usual case.  Another important difference is the fact that the
  point spectrum of $\widehat{N}_{\operatorname{ff},0}(H)(\tau)$ depends on $\tau.$ The
  family gap, defined in~\eqref{eqn119.224}, satisfies
  \begin{equation}
  \Gamma_0=  \Gamma(\lambda,\delta_0)>0;
  \end{equation}
  we assume that $\delta<\delta_0.$

  We let $\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)=\widehat{N}_{\operatorname{ff},0}(H)(\tau),$ which is given
  in~\eqref{eqn48.61}:
  \begin{equation}
   \hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)= \Delta^{(2)}\otimes\operatorname{Id}_{\Lambda^1\mathbb R^3}+\widetilde{Q}_1^{\epsilon,\mu}(\tau)+
    \widetilde{Q}_0^{\epsilon,\mu}+\omega^2(\kappa_0^2-\kappa^2),
  \end{equation}
  where $\Delta^{(2)}=-[\partial_{Y_1}^2+\partial_{Y_2}^2].$ Using the results
  in Appendix C of~\cite{VasyAsterisque} it suffices to show that
  there is a $C>0$ for which there exists a $\delta>0$ so that, if
  $\operatorname{supp}\phi\subset (\lambda-\delta,\lambda+\delta),$ then
  \begin{multline}\label{eqn144.224}
    \phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
        \left([\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau),Y\cdot\partial_Y]+2\tau^2+
          \tau\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon,\mu}_{10}\right)
        \phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\\\geq
        C \phi^2(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
  \end{multline}
  holds for all $\tau.$ The operator $\phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)$
  depends only on the spectrum of $\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)$ in the interval
  $(\lambda-\tau^2-\delta, \lambda-\tau^2+\delta).$ It therefore
  follows that from Proposition~\ref{prop2.224} that, for $\delta<\delta_0,$
  there is a $\tau'_{\max},$ so that
  \begin{equation}
      |\tau|>\tau'_{\max}\Rightarrow \phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)=0,
  \end{equation}
and therefore, for $|\tau|>\tau'_{\max},$~\eqref{eqn144.224} is
immediate. Because the family gap, $\Gamma_0,$ is non-zero, if
$2\delta<\Gamma_0,$ then $\operatorname{supp}\phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)$ lies
either in the continuous spectrum of $\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau),$ or in the
point spectrum, but not both. The arguments in the 2 cases are
somewhat different. We first consider the continuous spectrum; in this
case $\tau^2<\lambda+\delta.$

Given $\epsilon>0,$ with $\phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)$ supported in
the continuous spectrum, the fact that there is a $\delta>0,$ so that
 \begin{multline}\label{eqn146.224}
    \phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
        \left([\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau),Y\cdot\partial_Y]+2\tau^2\right)
        \phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\\>
        2(\lambda-\frac{\epsilon}{2}) \phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)^2
 \end{multline}
 is the classical 2-body estimate
 from~\cite{FroeseHerbst1,FroeseHerbst2}. Only the term
 \begin{equation}\label{eqn149.334}
   \tau q_0(\tau)= \tau\phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
        \widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon,\mu}_{10}
        \phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
  \end{equation}
requires further consideration. Because the support of
$\phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)$ lies in the continuous spectrum, we
claim that as $\delta\to 0,$ the norm of this operator tends to
zero. We prove this only in the case of the free space Laplacian.

Let $Q'=\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon,\mu}_{10};$ this is a compactly supported,
smooth matrix valued function, and let $\widehat{Q}'$ denote its Fourier
transform. For simplicity we replace $\phi(t)$ with
$\chi^{\delta}(t)=\chi_{[\lambda-\delta,\lambda+\delta]}(t).$ The
projection operator then takes the form
\begin{equation}
 \chi^{\delta}(\Delta+\tau^2)\psi=\mathcal F^{-1}\left[\chi_{D_{\tau}}(\xi)\widehat{\psi}(\xi)\right],
\end{equation}
where $D_{\tau}=B_{\sqrt{(\lambda+\delta-\tau^2)_+}}(0)\setminus
B_{\sqrt{(\lambda-\delta-\tau^2)_+}}(0),$ and $t_+=\max\{t,0\}.$ Using
the convolution theorem we see that
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal F(q_0(\tau)\psi)(\xi)=\chi_{D_{\tau}}(\xi)\int_{\mathbb R^2}\widehat{Q}'(\eta)\chi_{D_{\tau}}(\xi-\eta)\widehat{\psi}(\xi-\eta)d\eta.
\end{equation}

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality shows that
\begin{equation}
  \left|\langle\chi^{\delta}(\Delta+\tau^2)\psi,q_0(\tau)\psi\rangle\right|\leq
  \|\chi^{\delta}(\Delta+\tau^2)\psi\|\|q_0(\tau)\psi\|.
\end{equation}
The Parseval theorem and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality imply that
\begin{equation}
  \begin{split}
    \|q_0(\tau)\psi\|^2\leq &\|Q'\|_{L^1}^2\int
    \chi_{D_{\tau}}(\xi)
    \left[\int_{\mathbb R^2}\chi_{D_{\tau}}(\xi-\eta)d\eta\right]\left[\int
     \chi_{D_{\tau}}(\xi-\eta) |\widehat{\psi}(\xi-\eta)|^2d\eta\right] d\xi\\
  \leq &
  |D_{\tau}|^2\|Q'\|^2_{L^1}\|\chi^{\delta}(\Delta+\tau^2)\psi\|^2.
  \end{split}
\end{equation}
For bounded $\tau,$ the area  $|D_{\tau}|<m\delta,$ for a fixed
constant, $m,$ and therefore
\begin{equation}
  \left|\langle\chi^{\delta}(\Delta+\tau^2)\psi,\tau q_0(\tau)\psi\rangle\right|\leq
  m\delta|\tau||Q'\|_{L^1} \|\chi^{\delta}(\Delta+\tau^2)\psi\|^2.
\end{equation}
By choosing $\delta$ so that
$$m\delta\sqrt{\lambda+\delta}\|Q'\|_{L^1}<\epsilon,$$ this term can
be absorbed into the right hand side of~\eqref{eqn146.224}, proving
the existence of $\delta$ in these cases.

Recalling that $\delta<\delta_0,$ we are left to consider $|\tau|\in
(\sqrt{\lambda+\delta},\tau'_{\max}),$ with
$(\lambda-\delta-\tau^2,\lambda+\delta-\tau^2)$ intersecting only the
point spectrum of $\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau).$ Recall that all the point spectrum of
these operators is negative and is locally parameterized by analytic
functions $\{(\lambda_l(\tau),v_l(\tau)):l=1,\dots, N_{\tau}\},$ where
$N_{\tau}<J,$ for $|\tau|\leq |\tau'_{\max}|.$ The maximum number of
eigenvalues in an interval of length $2\delta$ is denoted by
$N^{\delta}_{\max}.$

As before we simplify the
discussion by working with the projections defined by
$\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2).$
A new difficulty that arises in the present case is that the point
spectrum of  $\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)$ depends on $\tau.$ If we make the
assumption that the eigenvalues of $\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)$ never cross, then
we can choose $\delta>0$ so that each interval
$(\lambda-\delta-\tau^2,\lambda+\delta-\tau^2)$ contains at most one
eigenvalue. It then follows from the virial theorem that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn170.502}
   \chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
        [\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau),Y\cdot\partial_Y]
        \chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)=0,
\end{equation}
therefore we are left to show that there is a positive constant $c$ so
that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn156.334}
  2\tau^2\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)+\tau
  q_0(\tau)>c\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2),
\end{equation}
see~\eqref{eqn149.334}. As $\tau^2>\lambda\in\mathcal I_M(c_0)$ it follows that 
there is a positive number $c_0$ so that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn202.700}
 \tau(2\tau+\dot{\lambda}(\tau))>c_0.
\end{equation}


                                                                
                                                                                
                                                           
                   
                                                                                
                 
                                                          
                                                                    
                   
                                              
                                  
                                            
                 
                                                                      
                                            
                                            

                                                                            
                                                   
                                                 
                                                          
                   
                                                                                
                                                             
                                                                                           
                         
                                                                     
                                                                              
                                     
                                                                 
                 
                                                  
                                                                         
                                                                                  
                   
                                                                     
                 


We now need to consider what happens if the interval
$(\lambda-\tau^2-\delta,\lambda-\tau^2+\delta)$ contains several
different eigenvalues. We first estimate of the contribution of the
$\widetilde{Q}^{\epsilon,\mu}_{10}$-term. As above
$\{(\lambda_j(\tau),v_j(\tau)):j=1,\dots,n\}$ are the eigenpairs with
$\lambda_j(\tau)\in(\tau^2-\lambda-\delta,\tau^2-\lambda+\delta);$ we
know that $n<N^{\delta}_{\max}.$ Since we are only considering a
single $\tau$ at a time, the functions $\{v_j(\tau)\}$ are an
orthonormal set, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eqn203.700}
  \langle \partial_{\tau}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)v_j,v_l\rangle=
  (2\tau+\dot{\lambda_j}(\tau))\delta_{jl}+(\lambda_j-\lambda_l)\langle\dot{v}_j,v_l\rangle.
\end{equation}
From which it follows that there is a constant, $M,$ so that
\begin{equation}
  \chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
 \tau
 \partial_{\tau}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)>
    \tau[ c_0-\delta M]\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2).
\end{equation}
Decreasing $\delta$ if needed, gives the desired lower bound.


We cannot use the virial theorem to estimate the left hand side
of~\eqref{eqn170.502}, but there is an approximate virial theorem that we
can use instead. We need to bound the
operator
\begin{multline}
  F_{\delta,\tau}=\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
        [\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau),Y\cdot\partial_Y]
        \chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)=\\
        \chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)
        [\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)-\lambda_0,Y\cdot\partial_Y]
        \chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2).
\end{multline}
Using the eigenpairs from above, the projection operator is given by
\begin{equation}
  \chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\psi=\sum_{l=1}^n\langle
  \psi,v_l\rangle  v_l,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 Y\cdot\partial_Y (\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)-\lambda_0)
 (\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\psi=
 \sum_{l=1}^n(\lambda_l-\lambda_0)\langle
  \psi,v_l\rangle Y\cdot\partial_{Y} v_l.
\end{equation}

A computation shows that
\begin{equation}
  \langle\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\psi,
  F_{\delta,\tau}\psi\rangle=
  -2\sum_{k,l=1}^{n}(\lambda_l-\lambda_0)\langle\psi,v_l\rangle
  \langle\psi,v_k\rangle\langle Y\cdot\partial_Y v_k,v_l\rangle
\end{equation}
Since all of the eigenvalues are less than $-\Gamma_0,$ the
exponential decay estimates for eigenfunctions show that there is
constant $M$ independent of $|\tau|\in [\lambda,\tau_{\max}]$ and the
particular eigenfunction so that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn165.334}
  \|Y\cdot\partial_Y v_k\|_{L^2}\leq M.
\end{equation}
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality then shows that, with another constant, $M',$
\begin{equation}\label{eqn166.334} 
  |\langle\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\psi,
  F_{\delta,\tau}\psi\rangle|\leq M'\delta
  \|\chi^{\delta}(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)\psi\|_{L^2}^2.
\end{equation}
Decreasing $\delta$ further completes the proof of the theorem.

  If $\lambda=\omega^2\kappa_0^2$ and the estimates
  in~\eqref{cntrst_ratio_est} hold, then, for small enough $\delta>0,$
  the estimates in~\eqref{eqn202.700} and~\eqref{eqn203.700} continue
  to hold for some $c_0>0.$ This shows that the Mourre estimate holds
  in this case as well.

title: Remark
body_md:
The assumption that $\Gamma_0>0$ allows us to avoid analyzing what
  happens if $\operatorname{supp}\phi(\hat{H}_{\operatorname{ff}}(\tau)+\tau^2)$ contains both
  continuous and point spectrum. It is easy to see that the
  approximate virial theorem,~\eqref{eqn166.334}, extends to the case
  $\Gamma_0=0.$ In particular, the estimate~\eqref{eqn165.334} does
  not require $\Gamma_0>0.$ Using the following lemma, we can extend
  our proof of this estimate to the case that $\Gamma_0=0.$ We leave the details of
  this extension to the reader; a proof of the Mourre estimate in much
  greater generality is provided in
  Appendix~\ref{MourreEstGenCase}.
                                       
                                                                     
  \begin{lemma}\label{lem1}
    Let $q$ be a  first order operator whose coefficients are
    supported in $B_R(0)$. There is a constant $C>0,$ so that if
    $v\in L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ is a solution to
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn168.334}
      (-\Delta+q)v=-\lambda v,
    \end{equation}
    for a $\lambda>0,$ then
    \begin{equation}
      \|r\partial_r v\|^2_{L^2(B_1^c(0))}\leq 4\|v\|^2_{L^2}+C\|\nabla v\|^2_{L^2(B_R(0))}.
    \end{equation}
    The constant, $C,$ is independent of $\lambda.$
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{remark}
    These estimates hold very generally for eigenfunctions of $N$-body
    Schr\"odinger operators, though the proof in the general case is
    considerably more technical.
  \end{remark}
  \begin{proof}
  As $q$ is compactly
 supported, the fact that $\lambda>0$ implies that $v$ and all of its
 derivatives are exponentially decaying. Let
 $\chi\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb R)$ be a monotone increasing function that is
 zero for $r<1/2,$ and $1$ for $r\geq 1.$ Integrating by parts we see
 that
 \begin{equation}
  \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty}|\chi^{\frac
    12}(r)r\partial_rv(r,\theta)|^2rdrd\theta=
  -\int_0^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty}\bar{v}\partial_r[\chi(r)r^3\partial_rv(r,\theta)]drd\theta.
 \end{equation}
 Expanding the derivative, using the equation~\eqref{eqn168.334} and integrating by parts in
 $\theta$ we see that
 \begin{multline}
  \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty}|\chi^{\frac
    12}(r)r\partial_rv(r,\theta)|^2rdrd\theta=-\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_0^{\infty}
  \chi(r)[|v_{\theta}|^2+\lambda r^3|v|^2]drd\theta\\
  -\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_0^{\infty}[2\chi(r)r^2\bar{v}\partial_rv+\chi_r
    r^3\bar{v}\partial_rv
    +\chi(r)r^3\bar{v}q v]drd\theta.
 \end{multline}
 The first integral on the right is non-positive, and the last two
 terms in the next integral are compactly supported. Applying the
 Cauchy-Schwarz and arithmetic-geometric mean inequality to the
 remaining term gives the conclusion of the lemma.
  \end{proof}

label: thm:non-product-prop-sing-WG
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:non-product-prop-sing-WG}
Suppose that $H$ is a wave guide 3-body operator, so $C_a$ for $a\neq
0,1$ is discrete. Suppose also that $\lambda=k^2>0$ and that the ideal
Mourre constant is $M'_1(\lambda)>0$. Suppose also that $(H-\lambda)u$
is Schwartz. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item
  Propagation of
singularities holds, i.e.\ $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)$ is a
union of maximally extended GBBs, and the same holds for all weighted
Sobolev wave front sets, $W^{m,l}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u).$
\item
  The high regularity radial estimates hold: if $R^+_{k^2,\operatorname{mf}}$ and
  $\cup_jR^+_{k^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}$ are disjoint from
  $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}^{*,-1/2+\delta}(u)$ for some $\delta>0$, they are also disjoint from
  $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}(u)$. The same holds with $R^+_{k^2,\operatorname{mf}}$ and
  $\cup_jR^+_{k^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}$ replaced by $R^-_{k^2,\operatorname{mf}}$ and
  $\cup_jR^-_{k^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}.$
\item
  The low regularity radial estimates hold: if a punctured
  neighborhood of $R^+_{k^2,\operatorname{mf}}$ and
  $\cup_jR^+_{k^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}$ is disjoint from
  $\operatorname{WF}_{3\operatorname{sc}}^{*,l}(u)$ for some $l<-1/2$, then so is $R^+_{k^2,\operatorname{mf}}$ and
  $\cup_jR^+_{k^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}$. The same holds for $R^+_{k^2,\operatorname{mf}}$ and
  $\cup_jR^+_{k^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}$ replaced by $R^-_{k^2,\operatorname{mf}}$ and
  $\cup_jR^-_{k^2,\operatorname{ff}_j}$.
\end{enumerate}
